sn5.2:1.2: For Pasenadi’s wife of the same name, see [mn90:3.1]() and note.
sn5.2:2.3: “Two-inch wisdom” (_dvaṅgulapaññā_), literally “two finger(-breadth’s) wisdom, is variously explained by commentaries as limited wisdom; or because women hold thread between two fingers; or because they test whether rice is cooked by pressing a grain between two fingers. Normally, _aṅgula_ with a number is a unit of length equal to the width of the middle finger, which is often a “small amount”. For example, the time past noon is measured when the sun’s shadow moves two inches ([pli-tv-kd22:1.10.16]()), which is the same distance the shadow moves each month (Arthaśāstra 2.20.42). The late literary text Bṛhatkathāślokasaṁgraha employs the same idiom, by a woman to dismiss women’s wit (22.35)—as so often, a woman makes the best misogynist—or by a man who muses that perhaps man like him are the real fools since they allow women to entice them (22.302–3).
sn5.2:2.4: It is Māra, not the Buddha, who doubts women’s capacity.
sn5.2:5.1: Somā’s verses at [thig3.8]() lack this verse.
sn5.2:5.3: Reading asmīti with other translators. But surely the Upanishadic echoes should be preserved here; it gets lost if we abbreviate “I’m”. She’s not just dismissing other conceptions of ultimate gender identity, but even the supposed post-gender Upanishadic self.
